fields.front: Conceptually, how do “receiving application” (MSH-5) and “receiving facility” (MSH-6) differ?
fields.back:
MSH-5 – Receiving application: the target system that should receive/consume the message.
MSH-6 – Receiving facility: the organization or site that owns that receiving application instance.

fields.front: Conceptually, how do “sending application” (MSH-3) and “sending facility” (MSH-4) differ?
fields.back:
MSH-3 – Sending application: the software/application instance sending the message (e.g., LABLIS).
MSH-4 – Sending facility: the organization or site the application represents (e.g., MAINHOSPITAL).

fields.front: Describe the components of the message type field (MSH-9).
fields.back:
<Message code> ^ <Trigger event> ^ <Message structure>
Example: ADT^A01^ADT_A01

fields.front: How are Z-segments named, and what are they used for?
fields.back:
Z-segments are locally defined extension segments whose names start with “Z” (e.g., ZBX).
They are used to carry site-specific data not covered by the base standard.

fields.front: In an HL7 v2 message, how are segments separated from one another?
fields.back:
Segments are separated by a carriage return (CR) character.
Example: MSH...<CR>PID...<CR>PV1...<CR>

fields.front: In MSH-9, what is the relationship between the message code and the trigger event? Give an example.
fields.back:
The message code describes the general type of interaction (e.g., ADT, ORM, ORU, ACK).
The trigger event describes why the message was sent (e.g., A01 admit, R01 result).
Example: ADT^A01 – an ADT message triggered by an A01 (admit/visit notification) event.

fields.front: List, in order, the default characters in MSH-2 (encoding characters).
fields.back:
^ – Component separator
~ – Repetition separator
\ – Escape character
& – Subcomponent separator

fields.front: What are the required fields in an MSH segment in HL7 v2.8?
fields.back:
MSH-1 – Field separator
MSH-2 – Encoding characters
MSH-7 – Date/Time of message
MSH-9 – Message type
MSH-10 – Message control ID
MSH-11 – Processing ID
MSH-12 – Version ID

fields.front: What character is used to indicate repeating values within a single field? Give an example.
fields.back:
The repetition separator is "~".
Example: two phone numbers in a repeating telecom field:
^PRN^PH^^^555^1234~^ORN^CP^^^555^9999

fields.front: What constraints exist on the choice of delimiter characters in an HL7 message?
fields.back: They must be printable from the allowed set, must not appear unescaped in data, and all communicating systems must agree on them (as defined in MSH-1 and MSH-2).

fields.front: What is the purpose of MSH-1, and where is it physically located in the message?
fields.back:
MSH-1 is the field separator. It is the single character immediately after "MSH".
Example: MSH|^~\&|... (here, "|" is MSH-1).

fields.front: What is the purpose of the escape character, and give one example of an escape sequence.
fields.back:
The escape character "\" allows delimiter characters to appear in data fields using escape sequences.
Examples:
\F\ – literal field separator (|)
\S\ – literal component separator (^)
\R\ – literal repetition separator (~)

fields.front: What is the third component of MSH-9, and why was it added?
fields.back:
The third component is the message structure (e.g., ADT_A01).
It explicitly identifies the structure definition (segment order, required/optional segments), since multiple trigger events can share the same structure.

fields.front: What MSH field indicates how the message should be processed (e.g., production vs test), and what are the usual values?
fields.back:
MSH-11 – Processing ID.
Common values:
P – Production
T – Training
D – Debug/debugging/test

fields.front: What MSH field indicates the HL7 version being used, and why is it important?
fields.back:
MSH-12 – Version ID.
It tells the receiver which HL7 v2 version (e.g., 2.3, 2.5, 2.8) the message follows, affecting segment definitions, data types, and requirements.

fields.front: What MSH field indicates the message type?
fields.back: MSH-9 – Message type.

fields.front: What MSH fields indicate the receiving application and receiving facility?
fields.back:
MSH-5 – Receiving application
MSH-6 – Receiving facility

fields.front: What MSH fields indicate the sending application and sending facility?
fields.back:
MSH-3 – Sending application
MSH-4 – Sending facility

fields.front: Which character is the default truncation character in HL7 v2, and what is it used for?
fields.back: # – It is the truncation character, indicating that the data has been deliberately cut off at that point (e.g., because of length limits).

fields.front: Which characters in an HL7 v2 message are considered delimiters/encoding characters?
fields.back:
Field separator – usually | (MSH-1)
Component separator – ^
Repetition separator – ~
Escape character – \
Subcomponent separator – &
(Plus, truncation character – default # – as an additional encoding character)

fields.front: Which MSH field is used to uniquely identify a message, and what property must it have?
fields.back:
MSH-10 – Message control ID.
It must be unique (within the sending system’s namespace) so receivers can detect duplicates and match acknowledgments.
